question: A large Automobile company has implemented SF for its Sales Associates. Leads flow from its website to SF using a batch integration in SF. The Batch job connects the leads to Accounts in SF. Customer visiting their retail stores are also created in SF as Accounts. The company has noticed a large number of duplicate accounts in SF. On analysis, it was found that certain customers could interact with its website and also visit the store. The Sales associates use Global Search to search for customers in Salesforce before they create the customers. Which scalable option should a data Architect choose to implement to avoid duplicates?
optionA: Create duplicate rules in SF to validate duplicates during the account creation process
optionB: Implement a MDM solution to validate the customer information before creating Accounts in SF.
optionC: Build Custom search based on fields on Accounts which can be matched with customer when they visit the store
optionD: Customize Account creation process to search if customer exists before creating an Account.
explanation:
Native Duplicate Management with matching and duplicate rules (A) catches matches at both the batch-integration insert and the manual store-created insert without custom code, the scalable low-maintenance choice. An MDM solution (B) is heavier infrastructure than needed here, and custom search/creation logic (C, D) duplicates platform capability with development effort.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is migrating data from legacy system to Salesforce. During data analysis it was discovered that data types of fields being migrated do not match with Salesforce data types. Which solution should a data architect use to ensure successful data migrations?
optionA: Migrate legacy data to a staging database for mapping then leverage an ETL tool to transform the data and load into Salesforce.
optionB: Export legacy data into the staging database and leverage stored procedures to transform data types before loading into Salesforce.
optionC: Migrate the legacy data leveraging an ETL tool to transform data types and load data into Salesforce.
optionD: Export legacy data into CSV files and leverage data loader to load data into Salesforce.
explanation:
An ETL tool transforms mismatched data types in flight — that is the T in ETL — so it maps legacy types to Salesforce types, cleanses, and loads in one pipeline (C). Standing up a staging database first (A) or writing stored procedures against one (B) adds infrastructure to do work the ETL layer already does. Data Loader (D) reads a CSV and writes it; it performs no type transformation, so a mismatched source would simply fail on load.
This is a tooling-judgment item: Salesforce documents the load mechanisms rather than ranking ETL against a staging database for this scenario.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Northern trail Outfitters (NTO) uses Sales Cloud and service Cloud to manage sales and support processes. Some of NTOs team are complaining they see new fields on their page unsure of which values need be input. NTO is concerned about lack of governance in making changes to Salesforce. Which governance measure should a data architect recommend to solve this issue?
optionA: Add description fields to explain why the field is used, and mark the field as required.
optionB: Create and manage a data dictionary and set up a governance process for changes made to common objects.
optionC: Create reports to identify which users are leaving fields blank, and use external data sources to augment the missing data.
optionD: Create validation rules with error messages to explain why the fields is used
explanation:
A maintained data dictionary documents each field's purpose and a change-governance process controls who can add fields and why, addressing the root cause of uncontrolled, undocumented metadata changes. Field descriptions/required flags (A) and validation rules (D) treat the symptom on individual fields but do not govern change, and reporting on blanks (C) measures the problem rather than preventing it.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Universal Containers (UC) owns a complex Salesforce org with many Apex classes, triggers, and automated processes that will modify records if available. UC has identified that, in its current development state, UC runs change of encountering race condition on the same record. What should a data architect recommend to guarantee that records are not being updated at the same time?
optionA: Embed the keywords FOR UPDATE after SOQL statements.
optionB: Disable classes or triggers that have the potential to obtain the same record.
optionC: Migrate programmatic logic to processes and flows.
optionD: Refactor or optimize classes and trigger for maximum CPU performance.
explanation:
Adding FOR UPDATE to a SOQL query takes a row lock on the selected records for the transaction, so a competing transaction must wait, preventing the lost-update race condition. Disabling automation (B) removes functionality rather than coordinating concurrency, moving logic to Flows (C) provides no pessimistic locking, and CPU optimization (D) addresses limits, not concurrency.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_locking_records.htm

question: UC has a legacy client server app that as a relational data base that needs to be migrated to Salesforce. What are the 3 key actions that should be done when data modeling in Salesforce? Choose 3 answers:
optionA: Identify data elements to be persisted in Salesforce.
optionB: Map legacy data to Salesforce objects.
optionC: Map legacy data to Salesforce custom objects.
optionD: Work with legacy application owner to analysis legacy data model.
optionE: Implement legacy data model within Salesforce using custom fields.
explanation:
Migrating a relational schema starts by deciding what actually needs to live in Salesforce rather than porting the whole database (A), mapping the elements that survive onto Salesforce objects (B), and then realising that model with custom objects and fields (E).
Option C is a strict subset of B — mapping to custom objects is one outcome of mapping to objects, since much of a legacy model lands on standard objects such as Account, Contact, and Opportunity. That is why B is keyed over C.
Be aware this item is loose: option D, analysing the legacy model with its application owner, is at least as defensible a third choice as E, and the two are not mutually exclusive. Treat A and B as the solid pair and the third slot as the item's weak point.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

corrected.note: Item defect: option C is a strict subset of keyed option B, and distractor D (analyse the legacy data model with its owner) is at least as defensible as keyed option E. The key is the exam's, but the third choice is not decidable from the stem.

question: UC has millions of Cases and are running out of storage. Some user groups need to have access to historical cases for up to 7 years. Which 2 solutions should a data architect recommend in order to minimize performance and storage issues? Choose 2 answers:
optionA: Export data out of Salesforce and store in Flat files on external system.
optionB: Create a custom object to store case history and run reports on it.
optionC: Leverage on premise data archival and build integration to view archived data.
optionD: Leverage big object to archive case data and lightning components to show archived data.
explanation:
On-premise/off-platform archival with an integration to surface the data (C) and big objects with Lightning components to display archived cases (D) both move volume off the transactional store while keeping 7-year data accessible. Flat files (A) make the data hard to query, and a standard custom object (B) still consumes storage and degrades performance at millions of rows.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has three systems: Salesforce, a cloud -based ERP system, and an on-premise Order Management System (OMS). An architect has been tasked with creating a solution that uses Salesforce as the system of record for Leads and the OMS as the system of record for Account and Contacts. UC wants Accounts and Contacts to be able to maintain their names in each system (i.e., "John Doe" in the OMS and "Johnny Doe" in Salesforce), but wants to have a consolidated data store which links referenced records across the systems. What approach should an architect suggest so the requirements are met?
optionA: Have Salesforce poll the OMS nightly and bring in the desired Accounts and Contacts.
optionB: Implement an integration tool to send OMS Accounts and Contacts to Salesforce.
optionC: Implement a Master Data Management strategy to reconcile Leads, Accounts, and Contacts.
optionD: Use the Streaming API to send Account and Contact data from Salesforce to the OMS.
explanation:
Three things in this stem only MDM delivers together: a different system of record per entity (Salesforce for Leads, the OMS for Accounts and Contacts), deliberate attribute divergence ("John Doe" in one system and "Johnny Doe" in the other), and a consolidated store that cross-references the same real customer across systems.
Point-to-point synchronisation (A, B) fails the second requirement outright — whichever side writes last flattens the other's name — and produces no cross-reference store. The Streaming API (D) delivers event messages one way; it reconciles nothing.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the integration mechanisms rather than naming MDM as the answer to this scenario.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers has millions of rows of data in Salesforce that are being used in reports to evaluate historical trends. Performance has become an issue, as well as data storage limits. Which two strategies should be recommended when talking with stakeholders?
optionA: Use scheduled batch Apex to copy aggregate information into a custom object and delete the original records.
optionB: Combine Analytics Snapshots with a purging plan by reporting on the snapshot data and deleting the original records.
optionC: Use Data Loader to extract data, aggregate it, and write it back to a custom object, then delete the original records.
optionD: Configure the Salesforce Archiving feature to archive older records and remove them from the data storage limits.
explanation:
Reporting Snapshots are the native mechanism for exactly this problem: they "let you report on historical data" by saving "tabular or summary report results to fields on a custom object" on a schedule. Snapshot the trend data, then purge the detail rows behind it (B). Scheduled batch Apex that rolls detail into a summary object and deletes the originals (A) reaches the same place under your own control.
Data Loader (C) extracts and loads; it does not aggregate, so that round trip cannot produce the summary the stem needs.
Option D is not the empty distractor it once was. Salesforce Archive is a real, separately purchased product whose policies "regularly offload inactive records, files, and attachments from production" and shrink the storage footprint. It is not keyed here because it addresses only half the requirement — storage — and does nothing for the historical trend reporting that is the other half.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.data_about_analytic_snap.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_analyticsnapshot.htm
https://www.salesforce.com/platform/data-archiving-solutions/

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation rejected option D on the ground that "there is no general native 'Salesforce Archiving feature'" — an invented absence. Salesforce Archive exists as a purchasable product with automated archiving policies that remove records from production.

question: UC is building a Salesforce application to track contacts and their respective conferences that they have attended with the following requirements: 1.Contacts will be stored in the standard contact object. 2.Conferences will be stored in a custom conference_ c object. 3.Each contact may attend multiple conferences and each conference may be related to multiple contacts. How should a data architect model the relationship between the contact and conference objects?
optionA: Implement a Contact Conference junction object with master detail relationship to both contact and Conference__c
optionB: Create a master detail relationship field on the Contact object.
optionC: Create a master detail relationship field on the Conference object.
optionD: Create a lookup relationship field on contact object.
explanation:
A many-to-many relationship requires a junction object with two master-detail relationships (to Contact and to Conference__c), letting each contact attend many conferences and each conference include many contacts while enforcing referential integrity. A single master-detail or lookup (B, C, D) can only model a one-to-many relationship.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a business that works directly with individual consumers (B2C). They are moving from a current home-grown CRM system to Salesforce. UC has about one million consumer records. What should the architect recommend for optimal use of Salesforce functionality and also to avoid data loading issues?
optionA: Create a Custom Object Individual_Consumer__c to load all individual consumers.
optionB: Load all individual consumers as Account records and avoid using the Contact object.
optionC: Load one Account record and one Contact record for each individual consumer.
optionD: Create one Account and load individual consumers as Contacts linked to that one Account.
explanation:
Salesforce names option D's design as an anti-pattern by its own worked example. Parent-Child Data Skew describes skew as "a large number of child records (10,000 or more)" on one parent, and illustrates it with "a customer with hundreds of thousands of contacts all assigned to one dummy account" — which is precisely what loading a million consumers as Contacts under a single Account produces. Every insert in the load contends for the same parent row, and every later visibility change forces Salesforce to scan the whole child set, so the design fails the stem's own "avoid data loading issues" test. Even the LDV guide's bucket-account workaround says to "set up several dummy accounts and distribute the contacts among them", never one.
One Account and one Contact per consumer (C) is the standard business-account B2C model when Person Accounts are not on the table — it is the same shape Person Accounts create internally. No parent carries more than one child, so there is no skew and no load contention, and both standard objects keep their full functionality.
A custom Individual_Consumer__c object (A) throws away everything that works on Contact. Loading consumers as Accounts with no Contacts (B) leaves nothing to attach activities, campaign members, or cases to.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

corrected.note: Key moved D to C. The deck keyed the single-bucket-account pattern, which is the exact configuration Salesforce's Parent-Child Data Skew page uses as its example of what not to do ("hundreds of thousands of contacts all assigned to one dummy account"), and which causes the load contention the stem asks to avoid. The LDV guide's own bucket workaround specifies several dummy accounts, not one.

question: Universal Containers (UC) is in the process of selling half of its company. As part of this split, UC's main Salesforce org will be divided into two org:org A and org B, UC has delivered these requirements to its data architect 1. The data model for Org B will drastically change with different objects, fields, and picklist values. 2. Three million records will need to be migrated from org A to org B for compliance reasons. 3. The migrate will need occur within the next two month, prior to be split. Which migrate strategy should a data architect use to successfully migrate the date?
optionA: use as ETL tool to orchestrate the migration.
optionB: Use Data Loader for export and Data Import Wizard for import
optionC: Write a script to use the Bulk API
optionD: Use the Salesforce CLI to query, export, and import
explanation:
The distinguishing requirement is transformation, not volume: Org B has different objects, fields, and picklist values, so every record has to be remapped in flight. An ETL tool is built for that — extract, transform against the new model, load — and can be re-run repeatedly as the mapping is refined across a two-month window.
Data Import Wizard (B) is limited to a small subset of objects and record counts and performs no transformation. A hand-written Bulk API script (C) and the Salesforce CLI (D) can both move three million records, but you would be building the mapping, value translation, and error handling that the ETL layer already provides.
This is a tooling-judgment item — Salesforce documents the mechanisms rather than ranking them for an org split.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Get Cloudy Consulting uses an invoicing system that has specific requirements. One requirement is that attachments associated with the Invoice__c custom object be classified by Types (i.e., ""Purchase Order"", ""Receipt"", etc.) so that reporting can be performed on invoices showing the number of attachments grouped by Type. What should an Architect do to categorize the attachments to fulfill these requirements?
optionA: Add additional options to the standard ContentType picklist field for the Attachment object.
optionB: Add a ContentType picklist field to the Attachment layout and create additional picklist options.
optionC: Create a custom picklist field for the Type on the standard Attachment object with the values.
optionD: Create a custom object related to the Invoice object with a picklist field for the Type.
explanation:
The classic Attachment object does not support custom fields, so the supported pattern is a custom object related to Invoice__c that stores each attachment reference plus a Type picklist, enabling grouped reporting. Options A-C all assume you can add or extend picklists on the Attachment object, which is not possible.
References:

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has adopted Salesforce as its primary sales automated tool. UC has 100,00 customers with a growth rate of 10% a year, UC uses an on-premise web-based billing and invoice system that generates over 1 million invoices a year supporting a monthly billing cycle. The UC sales team needs to be able to pull a customer record and view their account status, Invoice history, and opportunities without navigating outside of Salesforce. What should a data architect use to provide the sales team with the required functionality?
optionA: Create a custom object and migrate the last 12 months of Invoice data into Salesforce so it can be displayed on the Account layout.
optionB: Write an Apex callout and populate a related list to display on the account record.
optionC: Create a mashup page that will present the billing system records within Salesforce.
optionD: Create a visual force tab with the billing system encapsulated within an iframe.
explanation:
A mashup surfaces the high-volume billing/invoice data live from the on-premise system inside the customer record without copying 1M+ invoices/year into Salesforce, giving sales the consolidated view while avoiding storage cost and stale data. Migrating invoices in (A) consumes storage and goes stale, and an iframe tab (D) does not present the data in the context of the customer record.

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses Salesforce for tracking opportunities (Opportunity). UC uses an internal ERP system for tracking deliveries and invoicing. The ERP system supports SOAP API and OData for bi-directional integration between Salesforce and the ERP system. UC has about one million opportunities. For each opportunity, UC sends 12 invoices, one per month. UC sales reps have requirements to view current invoice status and invoice amount from the opportunity page. When creating an object to model invoices, what should the architect recommend, considering performance and data storage space?
optionA: Use Streaming API to get the current status from the ERP and display on the Opportunity page.
optionB: Create an external object Invoice__x with a Lookup relationship with Opportunity.
optionC: Create a custom object Invoice__c with a master-detail relationship with Opportunity.
optionD: Create a custom object Invoice__c with a Lookup relationship with Opportunity.
explanation:
With 12M invoices that live in the ERP and only need to be viewed, an external object (Invoice__x) via OData keeps the data off-platform, zero storage cost and always current, while still letting reps see status and amount on the Opportunity through an external/indirect lookup. Custom objects (C, D) would store 12M rows in Salesforce, and the Streaming API (A) is for event delivery, not displaying invoice history.

question: A customer wants to maintain geographic location information including latitude and longitude in a custom object. What would a data architect recommend to satisfy this requirement?
optionA: Create formula fields with geolocation function for this requirement.
optionB: Create custom fields to maintain latitude and longitude information
optionC: Create a geolocation custom field to maintain this requirement
optionD: Recommend app exchange packages to support this requirement.
explanation:
The Geolocation compound field stores latitude and longitude together and supports DISTANCE/GEOLOCATION functions and proximity queries natively. Separate plain number fields (B) lose the compound behavior, a formula field (A) cannot store user-entered coordinates, and an AppExchange package (D) is unnecessary for a built-in field type.

question: Universal containers is implementing Salesforce lead management. UC Procure lead data from multiple sources and would like to make sure lead data as company profile and location information. Which solution should a data architect recommend to make sure lead data has both profile and location information? Option
optionA: Ask sales people to search for populating company profile and location data
optionB: Run reports to identify records which does not have company profile and location data
optionC: Leverage external data providers populate company profile and location data
optionD: Export data out of Salesforce and send to another team to populate company profile and location data
explanation:
Leads arriving from many sources will be uneven no matter how carefully the forms are built, so completeness has to come from somewhere other than the source. An external data provider appends authoritative company profile and location attributes automatically as records land (C), which is the only option that scales with lead volume.
Asking reps to look the data up (A) and shipping exports to another team (D) both put a human in the path of every record. Reporting on blanks (B) measures the gap accurately and closes none of it.
This is a data-quality judgment item; Salesforce documents enrichment products rather than naming this as the answer.

question: Universal Containers has a legacy system that captures Conferences and Venues. These Conferences can occur at any Venue. They create hundreds of thousands of Conferences per year. Historically, they have only used 20 Venues. Which two things should the data architect consider when denormalizing this data model into a single Conference object with a Venue picklist? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Limitations on master-detail relationships.
optionB: Org data storage limitations.
optionC: Bulk API limitations on picklist fields.
optionD: Standard list view in-line editing.
explanation:
Collapsing Venue from a related object into a picklist on Conference trades relational integrity for a value list, and the consequences are all about how that value list behaves under volume. Loading hundreds of thousands of Conferences a year through the Bulk API puts every Venue value through picklist handling on insert (C), and a picklist is inline-editable from a standard list view (D), so a value can be changed in bulk by anyone with edit access and no relationship to protect it.
Master-detail limits (A) stop applying the moment the relationship is removed, and org storage (B) goes down, not up, when two objects become one.
Be aware this is a weakly constructed item. Neither keyed consideration is stated as a documented rule anywhere in Salesforce's picklist or Bulk API guidance, and the two remaining options are rejected on relevance rather than on any documented fact. The underlying design point — that twenty stable Venues are better modelled as a picklist than as a lookup that 20,000 records each point at — is sound and is documented, as concentrating that many children on one lookup target is textbook lookup skew.

question: Universal Containers (CU) is in the process of implementing an enterprise data warehouse (EDW). UC needs to extract 100 million records from Salesforce for migration to the EDW. What data extraction strategy should a data architect use for maximum performance?
optionA: Install a third-party AppExchange tool.
optionB: Call the REST API in successive queries.
optionC: Utilize PK Chunking with the Bulk API.
optionD: Use the Bulk API in parallel mode.
explanation:
PK Chunking is built for this exact volume. The Bulk API guide says it "splits bulk queries on large tables into chunks based on the record IDs, or primary keys, of the queried records", and recommends enabling it "when querying tables with more than 10 million records or when a bulk query consistently times out". At 100 million records both conditions apply.
Bulk API in parallel mode without chunking (D) still issues one query across the whole table, which is what times out. Successive REST queries (B) page through the same full scan more slowly. A third-party tool (A) runs on the same API and inherits the same limits.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/async_api_headers_enable_pk_chunking.htm

question: Due to security requirements, Universal Containers needs to capture specific user actions, such as login, logout, file attachment download, package install, etc. What is the recommended approach for defining a solution for this requirement?
optionA: Use a field audit trail to capture field changes.
optionB: Use a custom object and trigger to capture changes.
optionC: Use Event Monitoring to capture these changes.
optionD: Use a third-party AppExchange app to capture changes.
explanation:
Event Monitoring exposes login, logout, download, API, and package-install events through Event Log Files (and real-time event objects), purpose-built for this audit requirement. Field Audit Trail (A) tracks field value history, not user actions; custom triggers (B) cannot capture login/logout/download events; an AppExchange app (D) is unnecessary given the native capability.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/using_resources_event_log_files.htm
https://www.salesforce.com/platform/shield/

question: Universals Containers' system administrators have been complaining that they are not able to make changes to its users' record, including moving them to new territories without getting "unable to lock row" errors. This is causing the system admins to spend hours updating user records every day. What should the data architect do to prevent the error?
optionA: Reduce number of users updated concurrently.
optionB: Enable granular locking.
optionC: Analyze Splunk query to spot offending records.
optionD: Increase CPU for the Salesforce org.
explanation:
Moving users between territories rewrites group membership, and Salesforce "locks the tables holding group membership information during updates to prevent incompatible simultaneous updates" — which is where the lock errors come from. Granular locking is the mechanism that narrows those locks: it allows "some group maintenance operations to proceed simultaneously if there's no hierarchical or other relationship between the roles or groups involved", so separate role hierarchies and territory-free groups stop blocking each other.
Reducing concurrency (A) trades the error for a slower process. Splunk (C) and more CPU (D) address neither the lock semantics nor the tables involved.
One currency note: Salesforce now documents granular locking as the default behaviour rather than something an admin switches on, so on a current org the diagnosis matters more than the toggle.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_locking.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a requirement to create an Account plan object that is related to the Account object. Each Account plan needs to have an Account object, but the accessibility requirement of the Account plan is different from the Account object. What should an Architect recommend?
optionA: Create a custom account plan object as detail with Account as mater in a master-detail relationship.
optionB: Create a custom account plan object as detail with Account as master with additional sharing rules to allow access.
optionC: Create an account plan object with a lookup relations to Account without any validation rules to enforce the Account association.
optionD: Create an account plan object with a lookup relationship to Account with validation rules to enforce the Account association.
explanation:
A lookup relationship lets Account Plan keep its own OWD/sharing model (the differing accessibility requirement), and a validation rule enforcing a non-null Account makes the relationship effectively required. Master-detail (A, B) forces the plan to inherit the Account's sharing, violating the accessibility difference, and a lookup without enforcement (C) fails the 'each plan must have an Account' rule.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) provides shipping services to its customers. They use Opportunities to track customer shipments. At any given time, shipping status can be one of the 10 values. UC has 200,000 Opportunity records. When creating a new field to track shipping status on opportunity, what should the architect do to improve data quality and avoid data skew?
optionA: Create a picklist field, values sorted alphabetically.
optionB: Create a Master-Detail to custom object ShippingStatus__c.
optionC: Create a Lookup to custom object ShippingStatus__c.
optionD: Create a text field and make it an external ID.
explanation:
A restricted picklist enforces the 10 valid values (data quality) and avoids the lookup-driven data skew that would occur if 200,000 Opportunities all pointed at one of 10 ShippingStatus__c records (~20K children each). A lookup or master-detail (B, C) creates exactly that child-record concentration, and a free-text field (D) provides no value control.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/04/managing-lookup-skew-to-avoid-record-lock-exceptions
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: UC has a roll-up summary field on Account to calculate the count of contacts associated with an account. During the account load, SF is throwing an "Unable to lock a row" error. Which solution should a data architect recommend, to resolve the error?
optionA: Leverage data loader platform API to load data.
optionB: Perform Batch job in parallel mode and reduce Batch size
optionC: Perform Batch job in serial mode and reduce batch size
optionD: Defer roll-up summary fields calculation during data migration.
explanation:
Every Contact insert has to lock its parent Account so the roll-up summary can recompute. In parallel mode, several batches can hold contacts for the same Account at once, and one of them loses the race. Serial mode processes "one batch must complete before the next batch starts", and a smaller batch holds each parent lock for less time — which is the Bulk API guide's own remedy when lock timeouts survive batch reorganisation (C).
Parallel mode with smaller batches (B) shrinks the window without removing the overlap. The Data Loader (A) runs on the same APIs and changes nothing about locking. And there is no defer-roll-up-summary control (D) — deferral exists for sharing calculations, not for roll-ups.
The cheaper fix to reach for first, if you control the file: sort the Contacts by AccountId so all children of one Account land in the same batch, which the guide recommends before dropping to serial mode.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: US is implementing Salesforce and will be using Salesforce to track customer complaints, provide white papers on products and provide subscription (Fee) - based support. Which license type will US users need to fulfil US's requirements?
optionA: Lightning platform starter license.
optionB: Service cloud license.
optionC: Salesforce license.
optionD: Sales cloud license
explanation:
The requirement that decides this is fee-based support: service contracts and entitlements are Service Cloud functionality, and the Service Cloud feature license is what turns them on for a user. Case management and knowledge for the white papers come with it.
A Lightning Platform Starter licence (A) does not include the standard CRM service objects. Sales Cloud (D) is the wrong half of the product. The plain "Salesforce" user licence (C) is the base licence Service Cloud sits on top of, so naming it alone leaves the entitlement capability unaccounted for.
Licensing is the area of Salesforce that changes most often and is packaged commercially rather than documented as a rule, so verify the current bundle against Salesforce's licence documentation before relying on this.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The architect is planning a large data migration for Universal Containers from their legacy CRM system to Salesforce. What three things should the architect consider to optimize performance of the data migration? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Review the time zones of the User loading the data.
optionB: Remove custom indexes on the data being loaded.
optionC: Determine if the legacy system is still in use.
optionD: Defer sharing calculations of the Salesforce Org.
optionE: Deactivate approval processes and workflow rules.
explanation:
Two of the three are documented word for word in the LDV guide's Loading Data from the API: "Use the defer sharing calculation permission to defer sharing calculations until after all data has been loaded" (D), and "Disable Apex triggers, workflow rules, and validations during loads; investigate the use of batch Apex to process records after the load is complete" (E). Salesforce's own Extreme Data Loading series adds that sharing rules and complex relationships should be configured after the load rather than before it.
The time zone of the loading user (A) affects how date values are interpreted, not throughput. Whether the legacy system is still running (C) is a cutover question, not a performance one.
Option B is the item's weak point: removing custom indexes before a load is not among the pre-load steps Salesforce documents. Its published lean-configuration advice covers the sharing model, sharing rules, object relationships, workflow, validation, and triggers — indexes are discussed only as something to add for query speed.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/04/extreme-force-com-data-loading-part-2-load-into-a-lean-salesforce-configuration
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/05/extreme-force-com-data-loading-part-3-suspending-events-that-fire-on-insert

corrected.note: Answer stands as keyed, but option B is unsupported: the old explanation asserted that dropping custom indexes avoids per-insert index maintenance, and that step does not appear in Salesforce's documented pre-load configuration advice.

question: Universal Containers wants to develop a dashboard in Salesforce that will allow Sales Managers to do data exploration using their mobile device (i.e., drill down into sales-related data) and have the possibility of adding ad-hoc filters while on the move. What is a recommended solution for building data exploration dashboards in Salesforce?
optionA: Create a Dashboard in an external reporting tool, export data to the tool, and add link to the dashboard in Salesforce.
optionB: Create a Dashboard in an external reporting tool, export data to the tool, and embed the dashboard in Salesforce using the Canvas toolkit.
optionC: Create a standard Salesforce Dashboard and connect it to reports with the appropriate filters.
optionD: Create a Dashboard using Analytics Cloud that will allow the user to create ad-hoc lenses and drill down.
explanation:
The requirement is exploration, not display: drill down, build a view on the spot, add an ad-hoc filter from a phone. CRM Analytics (Analytics Cloud) is the Salesforce product built for that interaction model, with lenses created on the fly against a dataset (D).
A standard dashboard (C) renders components from saved reports with filters an admin defined in advance; a user cannot invent a new lens from it. The external-tool options (A, B) put the data and the security model outside Salesforce and hand the user a non-native mobile experience.
Product naming here has moved more than once — Wave, Einstein Analytics, Tableau CRM, CRM Analytics — so read option D as naming the Salesforce analytics product rather than a current brand.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bi_dev_guide_ext_data.meta/bi_dev_guide_ext_data/bi_ext_data_overview.htm

question: UC has a classic encryption for Custom fields and is leveraging weekly data reports for data backups. During the data validation of exported data UC discovered that encrypted field values are still being exported as part of data exported. What should a data architect recommend to make sure decrypted values are exported during data export?
optionA: Set a standard profile for Data Migration user, and assign view encrypted data
optionB: Create another field to copy data from encrypted field and use this field in export
optionC: Leverage Apex class to decrypt data before exporting it.
optionD: Set up a custom profile for data migration user and assign view encrypted data.
explanation:
Classic Encryption masks an encrypted custom field's value from anyone without the "View Encrypted Data" permission, and an export runs as the exporting user, so the export inherits that masking. Granting View Encrypted Data to the user that runs the weekly export is what makes the exported values readable.
The reason to build a custom profile (D) rather than reuse a standard one (A) is that standard profiles cannot be edited — permissions on them are fixed, so there is nowhere to add the permission. Copying plaintext into a second field (B) defeats the encryption entirely and doubles the exposure. Decrypting in Apex (C) rebuilds a permission the platform already has.
Worth noting: this item is about Classic Encryption, a legacy feature. Shield Platform Encryption handles the same problem through a different permission model.
References:
https://www.salesforce.com/platform/shield/
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to store product data in Salesforce, but the standard Product object does not support the more complex hierarchical structure which is currently being used in the product master system. How can UC modify the standard Product object model to support a hierarchical data structure in order to synchronize product data from the source system to Salesforce?
optionA: Create a custom lookup field on the standard Product to reference the child record in the hierarchy.
optionB: Create a custom lookup field on the standard Product to reference the parent record in the hierarchy.
optionC: Create a custom master-detail field on the standard Product to reference the child record in the hierarchy.
optionD: Create an Apex trigger to synchronize the Product Family standard picklist field on the Product object.
explanation:
A hierarchy is expressed by pointing each record at its parent, so a self-referential custom lookup on Product2 that references the parent Product (B) reproduces the tree from the master system, and each product's children fall out as its related list.
Pointing at a child (A, C) can only ever record one child per product, which is the wrong end of a one-to-many. Master-detail is not available here for a second reason: Product2 is one of the standard objects that cannot sit on the detail side of a master-detail relationship. The Product Family picklist (D) is a flat category, not a hierarchy, and no trigger makes it into one.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: UC has the following system: Billing system. Customer support system. CRM system. US has been having trouble with business intelligence across the different systems. Recently US implemented a master data management (MDM) solution that will be the system of truth for the customer records. Which MDM data element is needed to allow reporting across these systems?
optionA: Global unique customer number.
optionB: Email address.
optionC: Phone number.
optionD: Full name.
explanation:
Cross-system reporting needs a key that means the same thing in every system and never changes. A global unique customer number issued by the MDM hub is that key: it is the golden record's identifier, and each source system's record id maps to it, so a report can join billing, support, and CRM rows for one customer.
Email (B), phone (C), and full name (D) are all attributes a customer can change, share, or duplicate. Joining on any of them produces both missed matches and false ones, which is the problem MDM was brought in to solve.
An external ID field on the Salesforce side is where that key lives — external ID fields are indexed and support upsert, which is what keeps the mapping usable during integration.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: (Variant) Which three characteristics of a skinny table help improve report and query performance?
optionA: Skinny tables can contain frequently used fields and thereby help avoid joins.
optionB: Skinny tables can be used to create custom indexes on multi-select picklist fields.
optionC: Skinny tables provide a view across multiple objects for easy access to combined data.
optionD: Skinny tables are kept in sync with changes to data in the source tables.
optionE: Skinny tables do not include records that are available in the recycle bin.
explanation:
All three keyed properties are stated on the Skinny Tables page. Salesforce "can create skinny tables to contain frequently used fields and to avoid joins" (A) — the join avoided is between an object's base table and its custom-field table. "Skinny tables are kept in sync with their source tables when the source tables are modified" (D). And they "omit soft-deleted records", so recycle-bin rows never enter a scan (E).
Option C inverts the documented rule: "Skinny tables can't contain fields from other objects." Option B invents a capability — a skinny table is a denormalised copy, not an indexing mechanism, and multi-select picklists are not something it indexes.
Two details worth carrying: the documented cap is 200 columns, and you cannot build one yourself — "You can't create, access, or modify skinny tables yourself"; Salesforce Customer Support enables them.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_skinny_tables.htm

question: Get Cloudy Consulting needs to evaluate the completeness and consistency of contact information in Salesforce. Their sales reps often have incomplete information about their accounts and contacts. Additionally, they are not able to interpret the information in a consistent manner. Get Cloudy Consulting has identified certain ""key"" fields which are important to their sales reps. What are two actions Get Cloudy Consulting can take to review their data for completeness and consistency? (Choose two.)
optionA: Run a report which shows the last time the key fields were updated.
optionB: Run one report per key field, grouped by that field, to understand its data variability.
optionC: Run a report that shows the percentage of blanks for the important fields.
optionD: Run a process that can fill in default values for blank fields.
explanation:
The stem names two distinct qualities and each keyed option measures exactly one. Completeness is the share of records where a key field is empty, which a percent-of-blanks report gives directly (C). Consistency is whether the same real value is recorded the same way, which shows up when you group a report by a key field and see how many distinct values it has actually accumulated (B).
Last-modified dates (A) measure staleness, a third quality nobody asked about. Filling blanks with defaults (D) is remediation — it changes the data instead of reviewing it, and it makes the completeness measurement look better without any of the missing information having arrived.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: A custom pricing engine for a Salesforce customer has to be decided by factors with the following hierarchy: State in which the customer is located City in which the customer is located if available Zip code in which the customer is located if available Changes to this information should have minimum code changes What should a data architect recommend to maintain this information for the custom pricing engine that is to be built in Salesforce?
optionA: Create a custom object to maintain the pricing criteria.
optionB: Assign the pricing criteria within customer pricing engine.
optionC: Maintain require pricing criteria in custom metadata types.
optionD: Configure the pricing criteria in price books.
explanation:
Custom Metadata Types store the State/City/Zip pricing criteria as configurable records that Apex reads at runtime, so the pricing engine adapts to new values through deployable metadata changes rather than code edits. Hard-coding criteria in the engine (B) requires code changes, a custom object (A) puts the reference data in transactional storage, and price books (D) model product pricing, not a geographic decision hierarchy.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custommetadatatypes_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_custommetadatatypes.htm

question: Universal Containers wants to automatically archive all inactive Account data that is older than 3 years. The information does not need to remain accessible within the application. Which two methods should be recommended to meet this requirement? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Use the Force.com Workbench to export the data.
optionB: Schedule a weekly export file from the Salesforce UI.
optionC: Schedule jobs to export and delete using an ETL tool.
optionD: Schedule jobs to export and delete using the Data Loader.
explanation:
Both an ETL tool (C) and Data Loader (D) can run scheduled jobs that export inactive Accounts off-platform and then delete them, satisfying automatic archive-and-purge with no need for the data to remain accessible. Force.com Workbench (A) is a manual, unschedulable tool, and a weekly UI export (B) backs up data but never deletes it, so it does not archive.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_deleting_data.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.admin_exportdata.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) manages Vehicle and Service History in Salesforce. Vehicle (Vehicle__c) and Service History (Service_History__c) are both custom objects related through a lookup relationship. Every week a batch synchronization process updates the Vehicle and Service History records in Salesforce. UC has two hours of migration window every week and is facing locking issues as part of the data migration process. What should a data architect recommend to avoid locking issues without affecting performance of data migration?
optionA: Use Bulk API parallel mode for data migration
optionB: Use Bulk API serial mode for data migration
optionC: Insert the order in another custom object and use Batch Apex to move the records to Service_Order__c object.
optionD: Change the lookup configuration to "Clear the value of this field" when lookup record is deleted.
explanation:
Bulk API serial mode processes one batch at a time, preventing the parent-record lock contention that the weekly Vehicle/Service History sync hits within its short window. Parallel mode (A) is what causes the locking, moving records through an intermediary object (C) adds needless complexity, and changing the lookup delete behavior (D) addresses deletion, not load-time locking.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has built a custom application on Salesforce to help track shipments around the world. A majority of the shipping records are stored on premise in an external data source. UC needs shipment details to be exposed to the custom application, and the data needs to be accessible in real time. The external data source is not OData enabled, and UC does not own a middleware tool. Which Salesforce Connect procedure should a data architect use to ensure UC's requirements are met?
optionA: Write an Apex class that makes a REST callout to the external API.
optionB: Develop a process that calls an invocable web service method.
optionC: Migrate the data to Heroku and register Postgres as a data source.
optionD: Write a custom adapter with the Apex Connector Framework.
explanation:
The Apex Connector Framework lets you build a custom Salesforce Connect adapter that exposes the on-premise, non-OData source as external objects in real time without copying data or owning middleware. A REST callout in Apex (A) doesn't surface the data as queryable objects, copying to Heroku (C) violates the no-import goal, and an invocable web service (B) is not a real-time data-virtualization pattern.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_connector_start.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to capture information on how data entities are stored within the different applications and systems used within the company. For that purpose, the architecture team decided to create a data dictionary covering the main business domains within UC. Which two common techniques are used building a data dictionary to store information on how business entities are defined?
optionA: Use Salesforce Object Query Language.
optionB: Use a data definition language.
optionC: Use an entity relationship diagram.
optionD: Use the Salesforce Metadata API.
explanation:
A data dictionary needs both halves of the picture. An entity relationship diagram (C) records how the business entities relate to one another, which is the part no schema dump gives you. The Salesforce Metadata API (D) extracts the technical definitions — objects, fields, types, help text, and the data-classification attributes on each field — so the dictionary reflects what is actually deployed rather than what someone remembers.
SOQL (A) queries records, not schema, so it cannot describe a field that holds no data yet.
Be aware this item is loose: option B, a data definition language, is a perfectly ordinary way to capture entity definitions in a data dictionary outside Salesforce, and the stem asks about "the different applications and systems used within the company", not about Salesforce alone. B is rejected here only because the item is scoped to Salesforce metadata in practice.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

corrected.note: Item defect: distractor B (a data definition language) is a standard data-dictionary technique for a multi-system landscape, which is what the stem describes. The key is the exam's; the item is not cleanly decidable.

question: Universal Containers has multiple systems all containing and maintaining customer data. Although point-to-point integrations are in place, customers are complaining about consistency in the data. What solution should the data architect recommend?
optionA: Improve existing point-to-point integrations
optionB: Data cleanse each system
optionC: Perform a onetime synchronization to level set the built up inconsistencies
optionD: An MDM solution as the customer master, with centralized integrations to ensure consistency across all systems.
explanation:
Point-to-point integrations keep systems talking without ever deciding who is right, so every pair can drift independently and the customer sees a different answer depending on which system served them. An MDM solution acting as the customer master fixes the cause: one governed record, survivorship rules that decide which value wins, and centralised integrations so every system reads the same answer.
Improving the existing links (A) makes the same architecture faster at propagating disagreement. A one-time reconciliation (C) fixes today and nothing after it. Cleansing each system separately (B) leaves all of them independently authoritative, which is exactly the condition producing the complaints.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents governance practice rather than naming MDM as the answer here.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Universal Containers (UC) has implemented Salesforce, UC is running out of storage and needs to have an archiving solution, UC would like to maintain two years of data in Salesforce and archive older data out of Salesforce. Which solution should a data architect recommend as an archiving solution?
optionA: Use a third-party backup solution to backup all data off platform.
optionB: Build a batch join move all records off platform, and delete all records from Salesforce.
optionC: Build a batch join to move two-year-old records off platform, and delete records from Salesforce.
optionD: Build a batch job to move all restore off platform, and delete old records from Salesforce.
explanation:
A batch job that moves records older than two years off-platform and deletes them from Salesforce keeps two years of live data while reclaiming storage. Backing up all data off-platform (A) frees nothing unless deleted, deleting all records (B) destroys the needed two years, and option D's 'move all restore off platform' is incoherent for an archive.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_deleting_data.htm

question: UC is migrating data from legacy system to SF. UC would like to preserve the following information on records being migrated: Date time stamps for created date and last modified date. Ownership of records belonging to inactive users being migrated to Salesforce. Which 2 solutions should a data architect recommends to preserve the date timestamps and ownership on records? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Log a case with SF to update these fields
optionB: Enable update records with Inactive Owners Permission
optionC: Enable Set Audit fields upon Record Creation Permission
optionD: Enable modify all and view all permission.
explanation:
The 'Set Audit Fields upon Record Creation' permission lets the load preserve original CreatedDate/LastModifiedDate (C), and the 'Update Records with Inactive Owners' permission lets records keep owners who are now inactive (B). question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) plans to maintain contact preferences for customers and employees. NTO has implemented the following: 1. Customers are Person Accounts for their retail business. 2. Customers are represented as Contacts for their commercial business. 3. Employees are maintained as Users. 4. Prospects are maintained as Leads. NTO needs to implement a standard communication preference management model for Person Accounts, Contacts, Users, and Leads. Which option should the data architect recommend NTO to satisfy this requirement?
optionA: Create custom fields for contact preferences in Lead, Person Account, and Users objects.
optionB: Create case for contact preferences, and use this to validate the preferences for Lead, Person Accounts, and Users.
optionC: Create a custom object to maintain preferences and build relationships to Lead, Person Account, and Users.
optionD: Use Individual objects to maintain the preferences with relationships to Lead, Person Account, and Users.
explanation:
Salesforce's privacy model is built around a single standard entity rather than a preference field on each object. The Individual record is where a person's data privacy and communication preferences live, and the consent data model hangs the rest — authorization form consent, contact point consent, data use purpose — off it. Relating Leads, Person Accounts, Contacts, and Users to Individual records gives one preference store that behaves the same way for every actor type (D).
Custom fields per object (A) means four copies of the same preference and four places to keep them honest. A bespoke custom object (C) rebuilds Individual with none of the standard consent objects that already work with it. Cases (B) are a service construct and have no role in preference management.

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses the following Salesforce products: Sales Cloud for customer management. Marketing Cloud for marketing. Einstein Analytics for business reporting. UC occasionally gets a list of prospects from third-party source as comma-separated values (CSV) files for marketing purposes. Historically, UC would load contact Lead object in Salesforce and sync to Marketing Cloud to send marketing communications. The number of records in the Lead object has grown over time and has been consuming large amounts of storage in Sales Cloud, UC is looking for recommendations to reduce the storage and advice on how to optimize the marketing Cloud to send marketing communications. The number of records in the Lead object has grown over time and has been consuming large amounts of storage in Sales Cloud, UC is looking for recommendations to reduce the storage and advice on how to optimize the marketing process. What should a data architect recommend to UC in order to immediately avoid storage issues in the future?
optionA: Load the CSV files in Einstein Analytics and sync with Marketing Cloud prior to sending marketing communications;
optionB: Load the CSV files in an external database and sync with Marketing Cloud prior to sending marketing communications.
optionC: Load the contacts directly to Marketing Cloud and have a reconciliation process to track prospects that are converted to customers.
optionD: Continue to use the existing process to use Lead object to sync with Marketing Cloud and delete Lead records from Sales after the sync is complete.
explanation:
The prospects in these CSV files are marketing audience, not sales pipeline — nobody in Sales Cloud works them until one converts. Loading them straight into Marketing Cloud (C) puts the audience where the communications are sent from and keeps the growth out of Sales Cloud storage entirely; a reconciliation process brings across only the prospects that actually become customers.
Routing the files through CRM Analytics (A) or an external database (B) still needs a second hop into Marketing Cloud and adds a system to operate. Continuing to load Leads and delete them after each sync (D) keeps every one of the storage, automation, and audit costs the stem is trying to escape, and adds a bulk delete every week.
This is a cross-cloud architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the products rather than ranking these options.

question: Northern trail Outfitters (NTO) runs its entire out of an enterprise data warehouse (EDW), NTD's sales team starting to use Salesforce after a recent implementation, but currently lacks data required to advanced and opportunity to the next stage. NTO's management has research Salesforce Connect and would like to use It to virtualize and report on data from the EDW within Salesforce. NTO will be running thousands of reports per day across 10 to 15 external objects. What should a data architect consider before implementing Salesforce Connect for reporting?
optionA: Maximum number for records returned
optionB: OData callout limits per day
optionC: Maximum page size for server-driven paging
optionD: Maximum external objects per org
explanation:
External objects hold no data — every report row is fetched live by a web-service callout to the EDW at the moment the report runs. Thousands of reports a day across 10 to 15 external objects therefore turns directly into callout volume, and Salesforce meters it: "Depending on your qualified Salesforce organization edition, specific governor limits are in place for number of allowed callouts per hour and per day." Exceed them and the org becomes "temporarily unable to access external data sources through Salesforce Connect" — reporting stops org-wide, not just for the offending report.
The maximum records a query returns (A), the server-driven page size (C), and the ceiling on external objects per org (D) are all real limits, but none of them scales with how many times a day the reports run, which is the variable the stem puts in front of you.

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a very large and complex Salesforce org with hundreds of validation rules and triggers. The triggers are responsible for system updates and data manipulation as records are created or updates by users. A majority of the automation tool within UC'' org were not designed to run during a data load. UC is importing 100,000 records into Salesforce across several objects over the weekend. What should a data architect do to mitigate any unwanted results during the import?

optionB: Ensure duplication and matching rules and defined.
optionC: Import the data in smaller batches over a 24-hour period.
optionD: Bulkify the trigger to handle import leads.

question: Universal Containers is creating a new B2C service offering for consumers to ship goods across continents. This is in addition to their well-established B2B offering. Their current Salesforce org uses the standard Account object to track B2B customers. They are expecting to have over 50,000,000 consumers over the next five years across their 50 business regions. optionA: Use the Account object with Person Accounts and a new B2C page layout.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has a variety of customers that include householder, businesses, and individuals. The following conditions exist within its system: NTO has a total of five million customers. Duplicate records exist, which is replicated across many systems, including Salesforce. Given these conditions, there is a lack of consistent presentation and clear identification of a customer record. Which three option should a data architect perform to resolve the issues with the customer data?
optionA: Create a unique global customer ID for each customer and store that in all system for referential identity.
optionB: Use Salesforce CDC to sync customer data cross all systems to keep customer record in sync.
optionC: Invest in data duplicate tool to de-dupe and merge duplicate records across all systems.
optionD: Duplicate customer records across the system and provide a two-way sync of data between the systems.
optionE: Create a customer master database external to Salesforce as a system of truth and sync the customer data with all systems.
explanation:
A unique global customer ID stored in every system (A) gives referential identity across systems, a de-dupe/merge tool (C) resolves the existing duplicates, and an external customer master as system of truth synced to all systems (E) sustains a single consistent record. Salesforce CDC (B) syncs changes but doesn't dedupe, and two-way duplication (D) worsens the problem.

question: NTO need to extract 50 million records from a custom object everyday from its Salesforce org. NTO is facing query timeout issues while extracting these records. What should a data architect recommend in order to get around the time out issue?
optionA: Use a custom auto number and formula field and use that to chunk records while extracting data.
optionB: The REST API to extract data as it automatically chunks records by 200.
optionC: Use ETL tool for extraction of records.
optionD: Ask SF support to increase the query timeout value.
explanation:
A query timeout on a 50-million-row extract is a selectivity problem, and Salesforce publishes the technique that fixes it. Its LDV extraction guidance has you create an auto-number field with "Generate Auto Number for existing records" enabled, add a numeric formula field over it — because "you cannot use an index with comparison operators such as '<=' or '>' for the text-based auto-number field" — have Support index that formula field, then extract in ranges: WHERE ExportID__c > 1000000 AND ExportID__c <= 1200000. Each query stays under the index selectivity threshold, so none of them times out. That is option A, described almost word for word.
An ETL tool (C) is how you would orchestrate and schedule the extract, but on its own it issues the same unselective SOQL against the same 50 million rows and hits the same timeout — the chunking is the fix, not the tool. The REST API does not "automatically chunk records by 200" (B); that number is a query-locator page size and has nothing to do with query execution time. And the SOQL query timeout is not a value Salesforce Support raises on request (D).
On a current org, PK Chunking with the Bulk API does the same job with no custom fields, and Salesforce recommends enabling it "when querying tables with more than 10 million records or when a bulk query consistently times out". It is not among the options here, but it is what you would reach for first.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/06/extracting-large-data-volume-ldv-in-force-com
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/async_api_headers_enable_pk_chunking.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

corrected.note: Key moved C to A. Salesforce's own large-data-volume extraction guidance documents the auto-number plus indexed formula field as the chunking technique for exactly this failure, while an ETL tool by itself issues the same unselective query and hits the same timeout. The old explanation dismissed the documented technique as "fragile to build".

question: Universal Container has a Sales Cloud implementation for a sales team and an enterprise resource planning (ERP) as a customer master Sales team are complaining about duplicate account and data quality issues with account data. Which two solutions should a data architect recommend to resolve the complaints?
optionA: Build a nightly batch job to de-dupe data, and merge account records.
optionB: Integrate Salesforce with ERP, and make ERP as system of truth.
optionC: Build a nightly sync job from ERP to Salesforce.
optionD: Implement a de-dupe solution and establish account ownership in Salesforce
explanation:
Two different causes need two different fixes. The duplicates and the disagreement about which Account is right come from having no authority: integrating Salesforce with the ERP and naming the ERP the system of truth (B) settles that. The duplicates already in Salesforce, and the ones reps will create tomorrow, need a de-duplication solution plus clear account ownership so somebody is accountable for each record (D).
A nightly de-dupe and merge job (A) cleans up after a cause nobody addressed. A one-way nightly sync (C) is half of B — it moves data without establishing that the ERP's version wins.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents duplicate management and integration mechanisms rather than ranking these pairings.

question: During the implementation of Salesforce, a customer has the following requirements for Sales Orders: 1. Sales Order information needs to be shown to users in Salesforce. 2. Sales Orders are maintained in the on-premises enterprise resource planning (ERP). 3. Sales Order information has more than 150 million records. 4. Sales Orders will not be updated in Salesforce. What should a data architect recommend for maintaining Sales Orders in Salesforce?

optionB: Use custom big objects to maintain Sales Orders in Salesforce.
optionC: Use external objects to maintain Sales Order in Salesforce.
optionD: Use Standard order object to maintain Sale Orders in Salesforce
explanation:

question: Get Cloudy Consulting monitors 15,000 servers, and these servers automatically record their status every 10 minutes. Because of company policy, these status reports must be maintained for 5 years. Managers at Get Cloudy Consulting need access to up to one week's worth of these status reports with all of their details. An Architect is recommending what data should be integrated into Salesforce and for how long it should be stored in Salesforce. Which two limits should the Architect be aware of? (Choose two.)
optionA: Data storage limits
optionB: Workflow rule limits
optionC: API Request limits
optionD: Webservice callout limits
explanation:
Storing 5 years of status reports from 15,000 servers reporting every 10 minutes is bounded by data storage limits (A), and continuously ingesting that volume via integration is bounded by daily API request limits (C). Workflow rule limits (B) and web-service callout limits (D) are not the governing constraints for this storage/ingestion scenario.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has implemented Salesforce for its sales users. The opportunity management in Salesforce Is implemented as follows: 1. Sales users enter their opportunities in Salesforce for forecasting and reporting purposes. 2. NTO has a product pricing system (PPS) that is used to update the Opportunity Amount field on opportunities on a daily basis. 3. PPS is the trusted source within NTO for Opportunity Amount. 4. NTO uses Opportunity Forecast for its sales planning and management. Sales users have noticed that their updates to the Opportunity Amount field are overwritten when PPS updates their opportunities. How should a data architect address this overwriting issue?
optionA: Create a custom field for Opportunity amount that PSS updates separating the field sales user updates.
optionB: Change PSS integration to update only Opportunity Amount field when the value is null.
optionC: Change Opportunity Amount field access to Read Only for sales users field-level security.
optionD: Create a custom field for Opportunity amount that sales users update separating the field that PPS updates.
explanation:
The stem already names PPS as the trusted source for Opportunity Amount, so the design question is not who wins but how to stop the argument. Removing edit access to Amount from sales users through field-level security (C) does that at the platform level, and Forecasts keep reading the same standard Amount field they always did.
Moving either party to a custom field (A, D) leaves the standard Amount — the field Opportunity Forecasting actually uses — populated by only one of the two, so either forecasts lose the trusted number or they lose the sales users' input entirely. Writing only when Amount is null (B) hands authority to whoever types first, which is the opposite of what the stem says PPS is for.

question: UC needs to load a large volume of leads into Salesforce on a weekly basis. During this process the validation rules are disabled. What should a data architect recommend to ensure data quality is maintained in Salesforce.

optionB: Allow validation rules to be activated during the load of leads into Salesforce.
optionC: Develop custom APEX batch process to improve quality once the load is completed.
optionD: Ensure the lead data is preprocessed for quality before loading into Salesforce.
explanation:
Because validation rules are disabled during the weekly load, the only reliable way to maintain quality is to pre-process and validate the lead data before it enters Salesforce (D). question: Universal Containers (UC) is using Salesforce Sales & Service Cloud for B2C sales and customer service but they are experiencing a lot of duplicate customers in the system. Which are two recommended approaches for UC to avoid duplicate data and increase the level of data quality?
optionA: Use Duplicate Management.
optionB: Use an Enterprise Service Bus.
optionC: Use Data.com Clean
optionD: Use a data warehouse.
explanation:
Native Duplicate Management (A) is the platform answer: matching rules decide what counts as the same customer and duplicate rules alert or block at the moment of entry, in the UI and through the API, without code.
An enterprise service bus (B) moves messages between systems and a data warehouse (D) stores copies for analysis; neither compares two customer records or prevents a third.
Option C names Data.com Clean, which Salesforce has retired — it appears in the Past Product & Feature Retirements list, and its setup article no longer exists. Keep C as the keyed answer because that is what the item tests, but the current equivalent is a third-party enrichment and cleansing service or Data Cloud, and the point that survives is the design one: preventing duplicates at entry and standardising incoming values are two different jobs, and a duplicate rule only does the first.

question: Universal Containers uses Apex jobs to create leads in Salesforce. The business team has requested that lead creation failures should be reported to them. Which option does Apex provide to report errors from this Apex job?
optionA: Use Custom Object to store leads, and allow unprocessed leads to be reported.
optionB: Save Apex errors in a custom object, and allow access to this object for reporting.
optionC: Use Apex services to email failures to business when error occurs.
optionD: Use AppExchange package to clean lead information before Apex job processes them.
explanation:
Apex can report its own failures by email — a batch job marked Database.Stateful can accumulate failed rows across execute() calls and send them from finish() with Messaging.SingleEmailMessage, which puts the errors in front of the business team without anyone logging into Salesforce (C).
Storing the leads themselves in a custom object (A) records what did not get processed but reports no reason, and cleansing input with an AppExchange package (D) reduces failures rather than reporting them.
Be aware this item is weakly constructed. Option B — writing Apex errors to a custom object and reporting on it — is the pattern most production orgs actually use, because it survives inbox rules and supports trend reporting, and it is a direct answer to "errors should be reported to them". Nothing in the stem chooses between push and pull, so both B and C are defensible.

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_batch_interface.htm
