question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to ensure their data on 100,000 Accounts pertaining mostly to US-based companies is enriched and cleansed on an ongoing basis. UC is looking for a solution that allows easy monitoring of key data quality metrics. What should be the recommended solution to meet this requirement?
optionA: Use a declarative approach by installing and configuring Data.com Clean to monitor Account data quality.
optionB: Implement Batch Apex that calls out a third-party data quality API in order to monitor Account data quality.
optionC: Use declarative approach by installing and configuring Data.com Prospector to monitor Account data quality.
optionD: Implement an Apex Trigger on Account that queries a third-party data quality API to monitor Account data quality.
explanation:
The requirement has two halves — ongoing enrichment and cleansing of 100,000 Accounts, and easy monitoring of data quality metrics — and the item wants the declarative option that covers both rather than code that covers one. Batch Apex (B) and an Account trigger (D) both mean building and maintaining an integration, plus whatever reporting you write on top of it. Prospector (C) is the wrong half of the old product pair: it adds new records rather than cleaning existing ones.
The keyed answer names Data.com Clean, and that product no longer exists — Data.com appears in Salesforce's Past Product & Feature Retirements list, and its setup article is gone. As printed, this question has no correct answer on a current org. The durable point is the shape of the right solution: a configured, scheduled enrichment service that writes back match and fill status you can report on, which today means a third-party data quality service or Data Cloud rather than anything native.

question: Universal Containers is setting up an external Business Intelligence (BI) system and wants to extract 1,000,000 Contact records. What should be recommended to avoid timeouts during the export process?
optionA: Use the SOAP API to export data.
optionB: Utilize the Bulk API to export the data.
optionC: Use GZIP compression to export the data.
optionD: Schedule a Batch Apex job to export the data.
explanation:
The LDV guide's extraction advice points straight at the Bulk API: when a query could return over a million records, evaluate Bulk API 2.0's query capability. It runs asynchronously and returns results in batches, so the extract never sits inside a synchronous request waiting to time out (B).
The SOAP API (A) holds a synchronous connection open for a query it was never sized for. GZIP compression (C) makes the response smaller on the wire and changes nothing about how long the query takes to run server-side. Batch Apex (D) processes records inside Salesforce; it is not an export path to an external BI system.

question: For a production cutover, a large number of Account records will be loaded into Salesforce from a legacy system. The legacy system does not have enough information to determine the Ownership for these Accounts upon initial load. Which two recommended options assign Account ownership to mitigate potential performance problems?
optionA: Let a "system user" own all the Account records without assigning any role to this user in Role Hierarchy.
optionB: Let a "system user" own the Account records and assign this user to the lowest-level role in the Role Hierarchy.
optionC: Let the VP of the Sales department, who will report directly to the senior VP, own all the Account records.
optionD: Let a "system user" own all the Account records and make this user part of the highest-level role in the Role Hierarchy.
explanation:
One user owning every loaded Account is ownership data skew — Salesforce defines it as "a single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object" — and the cost lands on sharing recalculation: moving that user, or changing anything about their access, forces Salesforce to "adjust a very large number of entries in the sharing tables".
The documented mitigation is exact. First choice: "If you do have a compelling reason for assigning ownership to a small number of users, you can minimize possible performance impacts by not assigning the users to a role" — that is option A. If the user must have a role, the guidance is "Place them in a separate role at the top of the hierarchy", then "Don't move them out of that top-level role to avoid triggering sharing recalculations" — that is option D.
Option B does the opposite of what is documented. A role at the bottom of the hierarchy means every role above it inherits access to all of those records, so the sharing tables carry an entry for each ancestor and every recalculation walks the whole hierarchy. Option C is worse still: a real VP reporting to a senior VP sits mid-hierarchy and is a person whose role will actually change.
The same page adds a third rule worth remembering: "Keep them out of public groups that can be used as the source for sharing rules."
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_data_skew.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

corrected.note: Key moved A,B to A,D. Salesforce's Ownership Data Skew page says to place a heavy-owning user in "a separate role at the top of the hierarchy" when a role is unavoidable. The deck keyed the lowest-level role, which is the placement that maximises sharing-table entries because every role above inherits access to all the records.

question: Universal Containers keeps its Account data in Salesforce and its Invoice data in a third-party ERP system. They have connected the Invoice data through a Salesforce external object. They want data from both Accounts and Invoices visible in one report in one place. What two approaches should an architect suggest for achieving this solution? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Create a report in an external system combining Salesforce Account data and Invoice data from the ERP.
optionB: Create a report combining data from the Account standard object and the Invoices external object.
optionC: Create a Visualforce page combining Salesforce Account data and Invoice external object data.
optionD: Create a separate Salesforce report for Accounts and Invoices and combine them in a dashboard.
explanation:
A report in an external BI tool (A) reads Account data from Salesforce and Invoice data from the ERP directly, with no dependency on the external-object layer at all. A Visualforce page (C) queries the Account and the Invoice external object together and renders them as one view inside Salesforce.
Two separate reports side by side on a dashboard (D) is explicitly not the single combined report the stem asks for.
Option B is the interesting one. Salesforce does support reporting on external objects — it publishes an article titled "Salesforce Connect Support for Reports" — so a custom report type spanning Account and an Invoices external object is possible in principle. It needs an external lookup or indirect lookup relationship between them, which this stem never says exists, and reports that touch an external object are bounded in how many rows they fetch and depend on the ERP responding while the report runs. That is why A and C are the safer recommendations here, not because native reporting on external objects is impossible.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.platform_connect_considerations_reports.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands, but the old explanation asserted that "Salesforce cannot natively report across a standard object and an external object together" — an invented absence. Salesforce publishes "Salesforce Connect Support for Reports"; option B is possible given a lookup relationship, so this item has three defensible options rather than two.

question: As part of a phased Salesforce rollout. there will be 3 deployments spread out over the year. The requirements have been carefully documented. Which two methods should an architect use to trace back configuration changes to the detailed requirements? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Review the setup audit trail for configuration changes.
optionB: Put the business purpose in the Description of each field.
optionC: Maintain a data dictionary with the justification for each field.
optionD: Use the Force.com IDE to save the metadata files in source control.
explanation:
Traceability needs the reason to travel with the thing that changed. A field's Description holds its business purpose on the metadata itself, so it survives every deployment and is visible to whoever finds the field later (B). Metadata files in source control record exactly what changed in each of the three releases, and the commit history carries the why alongside it (D).
The setup audit trail (A) is a genuine record of what changed and when, but it captures no link to a requirement — it will tell you a field was created and by whom, never which documented requirement asked for it.
Be aware this item is loose: option C, a data dictionary holding the justification for each field, is a direct answer to "trace back configuration changes to the detailed requirements" and is a technique Salesforce's own governance guidance recommends. Nothing in the stem separates it from B, so three of the four options are defensible.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

corrected.note: Item defect: distractor C (maintain a data dictionary with the justification for each field) answers the stem as directly as keyed option B, and Salesforce's governance guidance recommends exactly that. The key is the exam's; the item is not cleanly decidable.

question: Universal Containers is establishing a call center that will use Salesforce. UC receives 10 million calls and creates 100 million cases every month. Cases are linked to a custom call object using lookup relationship. UC would like to run reports and dashboard to better understand different case types being created on calls to better serve customers. What solution should a data architect recommend to meet the business requirement?
optionA: Archive records to a data warehouse and run analytics on the data warehouse.
optionB: Leverage big objects to archive records and Einstein Analytics to run reports.
optionC: Leverage custom objects to store aggregate data and run analytics.
optionD: Leverage out-of-the-box reports and dashboard on case and interactive voice response (IVR) custom object.
explanation:
One hundred million cases a month is far outside what the transactional store is designed to report on, and big objects are the platform's answer to that shape — "consistent performance, whether you have 1 million records, 100 million, or even 1 billion", with "Historical archive" and "360° view of the customer" as their named use cases. Archive the case volume there and run the analysis on the analytics platform (B).
Out-of-the-box reports over standard Cases (D) are the thing that has already stopped working at this volume. Rolling everything into aggregate custom objects (C) means building and maintaining the aggregation yourself, and loses the detail behind it. Moving to a warehouse (A) works but takes the data off-platform, which the stem does not ask for.
One implementation detail: Salesforce does not have you report directly off a big object. View Big Object Data in Reports and Dashboards has you extract a representative subset — with Bulk API or batch Apex — into a custom object or dataset, and analyse that.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object_query_and_report.htm

question: (Variant) Universal Containers is experiencing frequent and persistent group membership locking issues that severely restricts its ability to manage manual and a automated updates at the same time. What should a data architect do in order to restore the issue?
optionA: Enable granular locking
optionB: Enable parallel sharing rule calculation.
optionC: Enable defer sharing calculation
optionD: Enable implicit sharing
explanation:
Persistent group-membership lock errors come from the sharing system locking "the tables holding group membership information during updates to prevent incompatible simultaneous updates". Granular locking is the mechanism that narrows those locks so "some group maintenance operations to proceed simultaneously if there's no hierarchical or other relationship between the roles or groups involved" — which is exactly what lets a manual update and an automated one run at the same time (A).
Deferring sharing calculation (C) is a planned bulk-window tool: you suspend recalculation, do the work, resume. It does not make two concurrent membership updates compatible. Parallel sharing rule recalculation (B) speeds recalculation of sharing rules, a different operation from group membership. Implicit sharing (D) is how Salesforce grants parent access from child records; it has no bearing on locking.
One currency note: Salesforce now documents granular locking as the default behaviour rather than something an admin turns on.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_locking.htm

question: NTO has decided to franchise its brand. Upon implementation, 1000 franchisees will be able to access NTO's product information and track large customer sales and opportunities through a portal. The Franchisees will also be able to run monthly and quarterly sales reports and projections as well as view the reports in dashboards. Which licenses does NTO need to provide these features to the Franchisees?
optionA: Salesforce Sales Cloud license
optionB: Lightning Platform license
optionC: Customer Community license
optionD: Partner Community license
explanation:
Franchisees tracking customer sales and opportunities are partners, not customers, and that distinction is what the licence split is built on: the Partner Community licence is the external licence that carries leads, opportunities, campaigns, and quotes, along with reports and dashboards in the site. Customer Community (C) is built for service — cases, knowledge, orders — and does not extend to the sales objects these franchisees need.
A full Salesforce licence (A) is for internal employees and would not be bought a thousand times over for external franchisees. A Lightning Platform licence (B) gives custom apps without the standard CRM sales objects.
Licensing is packaged commercially and changes often, so confirm the current Experience Cloud licence comparison before relying on this.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has deployed Salesforce to manage Marketing. Sales, and Support efforts in a multi-system ERP environment After reaching the limits of native reports & dashboards. UC leadership is looking to understand what options can be used to provide more analytical insights. What two approaches should an architect recommend? Choose 2 answers
optionA: AppExchange Apps
optionB: Wave Analytics
optionC: Weekly Snapshots
optionD: Setup Audit Trails
explanation:
Once native reports and dashboards have hit their ceiling, the two directions that add real analytical capability are the Salesforce analytics platform — CRM Analytics, named here by its older brand — which brings datasets, lenses, and exploration beyond what a report can express (B), and purpose-built analytics apps from AppExchange that package models and dashboards for a domain (A).
Weekly snapshots (C) are a way to accumulate history for trending; useful, but they add data, not analytical capability. The Setup Audit Trail (D) records configuration changes and has nothing to do with business insight.
The product in option B has been renamed several times — Wave, Einstein Analytics, Tableau CRM, CRM Analytics — so read it as naming the Salesforce analytics platform rather than a current brand.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bi_dev_guide_ext_data.meta/bi_dev_guide_ext_data/bi_ext_data_overview.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_analyticsnapshot.htm

question: North Trail Outfitters (NTD) is in the process of evaluating big objects to store large amounts of asset data from an external system. NTO will need to report on this asset data weekly. Which two native tools should a data architect recommend to achieve this reporting requirement?
optionA: Standard reports and dashboards
optionB: Async SOQL with a custom object
optionC: Standard SOQL queries
optionD: Einstein Analytics
explanation:
Big objects sit outside the standard reporting path. Salesforce's own guidance is that at this scale "it's not practical to build reports or dashboards directly from that data" — you extract a representative subset into a custom object and report on that (B), or feed the analytics platform and analyse it there (D). Standard reports and dashboards (A) cannot be pointed at a big object, and synchronous SOQL (C) is confined to the big object's index fields with equality and range filters only, which is a lookup mechanism rather than a reporting one.
Read option B for the pattern, not the tool it names. **Async SOQL was retired in Summer '23**: Salesforce's retirement notice states "You must use the Bulk API or batch Apex to query or report on custom Big Objects after your org gets upgraded to the Summer '23 release." The aggregate-into-a-custom-object approach is still right; the mechanism is now Bulk API or batch Apex.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000394892&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object_query_and_report.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.soql_sosl.meta/soql_sosl/big_object_querying.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands as keyed, but keyed option B names Async SOQL, which Salesforce retired in Summer '23 and replaced with Bulk API or batch Apex for querying and reporting on big objects.

question: Universal Containers is looking to use Salesforce to manage their sales organization. They will be migrating legacy account data from two aging systems into Salesforce. Which two design considerations should an architect take to minimize data duplication? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Use a workflow to check and prevent duplicates.
optionB: Clean data before importing to Salesforce.
optionC: Use Salesforce matching and duplicate rules.
optionD: Import the data concurrently.
explanation:
Cleansing and de-duplicating in the source/staging step before load (B) removes duplicates and bad data up front, and native matching/duplicate rules (C) catch cross-system collisions at insert time. Workflow rules (A) cannot block or merge duplicates, and concurrent imports (D) increase, rather than reduce, the chance of creating duplicates.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Two million Opportunities need to be loaded in different batches into Salesforce using the Bulk API in parallel mode. What should an Architect consider when loading the Opportunity records?
optionA: Use the Name field values to sort batches.
optionB: Order batches by Auto-number field.
optionC: Create indexes on Opportunity object text fields.
optionD: Group batches by the AccountId field.
explanation:
Grouping Opportunity records by AccountId so all children of the same Account fall in one batch prevents two parallel batches from locking the same parent Account, avoiding lock contention in parallel mode. Sorting by Name or Auto-number (A, B) scatters children of the same parent across batches, and text indexes (C) do nothing for write-time locking.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing its new Internet of Things technology, which consists of smart containers that provide information on container temperature and humidity updated every 10 minutes back to UC. There are roughly 10,000 containers equipped with this technology with the number expected to increase to 50,000 across the next five years. It is essential that Salesforce user have access to current and historical temperature and humidity data for each container. What is the recommended solution?
optionA: Create new custom fields for temperature and humidity in the existing Container custom object, as well as an external ID field that is unique for each container. These custom fields are updated when a new measure is received.
optionB: Create a new Container Reading custom object, which is created when a new measure is received for a specific container. The Container Reading custom object has a master-detail relationship to the container object.
optionC: Create a new Lightning Component that displays last humidity and temperature data for a specific container and can also display historical trends obtaining relevant data from UC's existing data warehouse.
optionD: Create a new Container Reading custom object with a master-detail relationship to Container which is created when a new measure is received for a specific container. Implement an archiving process that runs every hour.
explanation:
Overwriting temperature and humidity on the Container record (A) keeps only the latest value, and the stem requires historical readings as well as current ones — so the readings have to be their own records. A Container Reading child object gives that, and the archiving process is what keeps it viable: 50,000 containers reporting every ten minutes is 144 readings per container per day, so each Container passes 10,000 children in under three months. Salesforce's own guidance is to "Distribute child records so that no parent has more than 10,000 child records", which makes an archiving process part of the design rather than an optimisation (D).
Option B is the same model without that archiving, so it walks into parent-child data skew on every container. A Lightning component reading from the warehouse (C) solves the display problem and never stores the current reading in Salesforce at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

question: To avoid creating duplicate Contacts, a customer frequently uses Data Loader to upsert Contact records into Salesforce. What common error should the data architect be aware of when using upsert?
optionA: Errors with duplicate external Id values within the same CSV file.
optionB: Errors with records being updated and inserted in the same CSV file.
optionC: Errors when a duplicate Contact name is found cause upsert to fail.
optionD: Errors with using the wrong external Id will cause the load to fail.
explanation:
Upsert matches on the External ID; if the same file contains two rows with the same External ID value, Data Loader cannot decide which record to map to and throws a 'Duplicate value found / Duplicate Id Specified' error for those rows. Mixing inserts and updates in one file (B) is exactly what upsert is designed to handle, so it is not an error.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Which two aspects of data does an Enterprise data governance program aim to improve?
optionA: Data integrity
optionB: Data distribution
optionC: Data usability
optionD: Data modeling
explanation:
A governance programme exists to make data trustworthy and useful. Integrity (A) is the trustworthy half — accuracy, consistency, and validity of the values themselves. Usability (C) is the other half — data that people can find, interpret the same way, and reuse, which is why governance produces things like a data dictionary and field-level classification rather than only validation rules.
Distribution (B) and modelling (D) are how the data gets built and moved. Both are shaped by governance decisions; neither is an outcome the programme is measured on.
This is a definitional item drawn from general data-governance practice rather than a Salesforce rule.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: DreamHouse Realty has a Salesforce org that is used to manage Contacts. What are two things an Architect should consider using to maintain data quality in this situation? (Choose two.)
optionA: Use the private sharing model.
optionB: Use Salesforce duplicate management.
optionC: Use validation rules on new record create and edit.
optionD: Use workflow to delete duplicate records.
explanation:
Duplicate Management (B) prevents/flags duplicate Contacts via matching and duplicate rules, and validation rules (C) enforce data-entry standards on create and edit. A private sharing model (A) controls visibility, not quality, and workflow rules (D) cannot delete records.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing a new customer categorization process where customers should be assigned to a Gold, Silver, or Bronze category if they've purchased UC's new support service. Customers are expected to be evenly distributed across all three categories. Currently, UC has around 500,000 customers, and is expecting 1% of existing non-categorized customers to purchase UC's new support service every month over the next five years. What is the recommended solution to ensure long-term performance, bearing in mind the above requirements?
optionA: Implement a new global picklist custom field with Gold, Silver, and Bronze values and enable it in Account.
optionB: Implement a new picklist custom field in the Account object with Gold, Silver, and Bronze values.
optionC: Implement a new Categories custom object and a master-detail relationship from Account to Category.
optionD: Implement a new Categories custom object and create a lookup field from Account to Category.
explanation:
A picklist with three values stores the category directly on the Account, filters/groups easily, and avoids the data skew that a Category object would create (with ~167K accounts pointing at each of three Category records). A master-detail or lookup to a 3-record Category object (C, D) concentrates hundreds of thousands of children under each parent, causing sharing/lock performance problems at scale.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/04/managing-lookup-skew-to-avoid-record-lock-exceptions
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm

question: Get Cloud Consulting needs to integrate two different systems with customer records into the Salesforce Account object. So that no duplicate records are created in Salesforce, Master Data Management will be used. An Architect needs to determine which system is the system of record on a field level. What should the Architect do to achieve this goal?
optionA: Master Data Management systems determine system of record, and the Architect doesn't have to think about what data is controlled by what system.
optionB: Key stakeholders should review any fields that share the same purpose between systems to see how they will be used in Salesforce.
optionC: The database schema for each external system should be reviewed, and fields with different names should always be separate fields in Salesforce.
optionD: Any field that is an input field in either external system will be overwritten by the last record integrated and can never have a system of record.
explanation:
MDM enforces a decision about which system owns a field; it does not make that decision. Two systems whose fields share a purpose have to be compared by the people who know how each is populated and what the field will be used for in Salesforce, and that review is what produces a field-level system of record (B).
Option A hands the judgment to the tool, which is precisely the step MDM cannot do for you. Option C makes a naming difference into a schema difference, which manufactures duplicate fields for the same concept. Option D describes last-writer-wins and then declares the problem unsolvable — the ungoverned outcome the whole exercise exists to prevent.
This is a governance-judgment item; Salesforce documents the mechanisms rather than the review.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers has a large number of Opportunity fields (100) that they want to track field history on. Which two actions should an architect perform in order to meet this requirement? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Create a custom object to store a copy of the record when changed.
optionB: Create a custom object to store the previous and new field values.
optionC: Use Analytic Snapshots to store a copy of the record when changed.
optionD: Select the 100 fields in the Opportunity Set History Tracking page.
explanation:
Standard field history tracking cannot reach 100 fields — "The default limit is 20 fields per object" — and what it does capture is retained for a bounded window rather than indefinitely. So option D is not a configuration anyone can save, and the requirement has to be met by writing the history yourself.
Both remaining approaches do that. A custom object that stores a copy of the record whenever it changes (A) preserves the whole state at each point in time. A custom object that logs the previous and new values for each changed field (B) stores the deltas, which is closer to what field history actually is and far cheaper per change. Either is populated from an Apex trigger.
Reporting snapshots (C) run on a schedule and capture report rows, so they sample state at fixed intervals — they would miss every change that happens and reverses between two runs.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000383595&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_analyticsnapshot.htm

question: Universal Containers has received complaints that customers are being called by multiple Sales Reps where the second Sales Rep that calls is unaware of the previous call by their coworker. What is a data quality problem that could cause this?
optionA: Missing phone number on the Contact record.
optionB: Customer phone number has changed on the Contact record.
optionC: Duplicate Contact records exist in the system.
optionD: Duplicate Activity records on a Contact.
explanation:
Duplicate Contact records split a customer's activity history across multiple records, so a rep working one duplicate cannot see the call logged on the other, producing the uncoordinated duplicate-call symptom. A missing or changed phone number (A, B) would prevent or misdirect calls, not cause uncoordinated duplicate calls, and duplicate activities on one contact (D) would be visible together.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm

question: (Variant) A data architect is working with a large B2C retailer and needs to model the consumer account structure in Salesforce. What standard feature should be selected in this scenario?
optionA: Individual Accounts
optionB: Account Contact
optionC: Contacts
optionD: Person Accounts
explanation:
A person account "stores information about individual consumers" — one record that carries both account and contact attributes, which is what a B2C model needs when there is no employing organisation to hang a Contact from (D).
Contacts alone (C), or an account-and-contact pair (B), both require a parent Account, and inventing one shared parent for consumers produces the parent-child data skew Salesforce warns against. "Individual Accounts" (A) is not a Salesforce feature; the standard object named Individual exists, but it holds data privacy and consent preferences, not the consumer's account record.
Before enabling this in a real org, read Considerations for Using Person Accounts — the feature changes Account behaviour org-wide and cannot be turned off.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.account_person_behavior.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) requires 2 years of customer related cases to be available on SF for operational reporting. Any cases older than 2 years and upto 7 years need to be available on demand to the Service agents. UC creates 5 million cases per yr. Which 2 data archiving strategies should a data architect recommend? Choose 2 options:
optionA: Use custom objects for cases older than 2 years and use nightly batch to move them.
optionB: Sync cases older than 2 years to an external database, and provide access to Service agents to the database
optionC: Use big objects for cases older than 2 years, and use nightly batch to move them.
optionD: Use Heroku and external objects to display cases older than 2 years and bulk API to hard delete from Salesforce.
explanation:
Big objects (C) hold the 2-7 year archive on-platform at scale without storage/performance penalties, while Heroku + external objects (D) surface archived cases on demand and Bulk API hard delete reclaims storage from the transactional store. A standard custom object (A) still consumes storage at 25M+ rows, and exporting to a raw external DB without virtualization (B) makes on-demand in-Salesforce access harder for agents.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_deleting_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

question: A large insurance provider is looking to implement Salesforce. The following exist. 1. Multiple channel for lead acquisition 2. Duplication leads across channels 3. Poor customer experience and higher costs On analysis, it found that there are duplicate leads that are resulting to mitigate the issues?
optionA: Build process is manually search and merge duplicates.
optionB: Standardize lead information across all channels.
optionC: Build a custom solution to identify and merge duplicate leads.
optionD: Implement a third-party solution to clean and enrich lead data.
optionE: Implement de-duplication strategy to prevent duplicate leads
explanation:
Standardizing lead capture formats/fields across channels (B) reduces the inconsistencies that create near-duplicates, a third-party cleanse/enrich service (D) validates and corrects lead data at scale, and a de-duplication strategy using native matching/duplicate rules (E) prevents duplicates at entry. Manual search-and-merge (A) and a bespoke custom build (C) are costly, slow, and hard to maintain.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Developers at Universal Containers need to build a report for the business which displays Accounts opened in the past year grouped by industry. This report will also include information from contacts, opportunities, and orders. There are several million Accounts in the system. Which two options should be recommended to make this report perform well and satisfy the business need?
optionA: Use triggers to populate denormalized related fields on the Account.
optionB: Use formula fields to surface information from related entities on the report.
optionC: Use unbounded date ranges to filter the report.
optionD: Use an indexed date field with bounded date filters.
explanation:
The LDV guide's reporting advice is to cut both joins and rows. Denormalising the related data onto the Account with triggers (A) is its "De-normalize data when practical… Use summarized data stored on the parent record for the report" — the report then reads one object instead of joining Contact, Opportunity, and Order across several million Accounts. An indexed date field with a bounded filter (D) is the other half: "Use report filters that emphasize the use of standard or custom indexed fields", and a bounded range is what lets the optimizer use that index.
Cross-object formula fields (B) are evaluated at query time on every row, so they add the join cost back that denormalising removed. Unbounded date ranges (C) defeat index selectivity outright and send the query to a full scan.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_reporting.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: Universal Containers is exporting 40 million Account records from Salesforce using Informatica Cloud. The ETL tool fails and the query log indicates a full table scan time-out failure. What is the recommended solution?
optionA: Modify the export job header to specify Export-in-Parallel.
optionB: Modify the export query with LIMIT clause with Batch size 10,000.
optionC: Modify the export query that includes standard index fields(s).
optionD: Modify the export job header to specify Sforce-Enable-PKChunking.
explanation:
Enabling PK Chunking via the Sforce-Enable-PKChunking header splits the 40M-row extract into ID-range batches the Bulk API processes sequentially, avoiding the full-table-scan timeout. Adding indexed fields to the query (C) can help selectivity but doesn't address extracting the entire table, and a generic LIMIT/parallel tweak (A, B) doesn't solve the scan timeout at this volume.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/async_api_headers_enable_pk_chunking.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has recently implemented Salesforce to track opportunities across all their regions. NTO sales teams across all regions have historically managed their sales process in Microsoft Excel. NTO sales teams are complaining that their data from the Excel files were not migrated as part of the implementation and NTO is now facing low Salesforce adoption. What should a data architect recommend to increase Salesforce adoption?
optionA: Use the Excel connector to Salesforce to sync data from individual Excel files.
optionB: Define a standard mapping and train sales users to import opportunity data.
optionC: Load data in external database and provide access to database to sales users.
optionD: Create a chatter group and upload all Excel files to the group.
explanation:
The adoption problem here is that the reps' actual working data never arrived. Defining a standard field mapping from the spreadsheets to Opportunity and training the teams to import their own data (B) puts that history into Salesforce and, just as importantly, leaves the reps able to do it again without filing a ticket.
An Excel connector syncing individual files (A) keeps the spreadsheets authoritative, which is the habit the implementation was meant to end. An external database (C) adds a system nobody asked for. Uploading the files to a Chatter group (D) stores them as attachments — not reportable, not forecastable, and no better than the shared drive they came from.
This is a change-adoption judgment item rather than a documented rule.

question: UC is using SF CRM. UC sales managers are complaining about data quality and would like to monitor and measure data quality. Which 2 solutions should a data architect recommend to monitor and measure data quality? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use custom objects and fields to identify issues.
optionB: Review data quality reports and dashboards.
optionC: Install and run data quality analysis dashboard app
optionD: Export data and check for data completeness outside of Salesforce.
explanation:
Monitoring means something that keeps producing numbers without anyone remembering to run it. Reports and dashboards built on the quality dimensions the org cares about (B) do that natively, and the Data Quality Analysis Dashboards app from Salesforce Labs (C) packages the same idea — formula fields that score completeness on Leads, Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities and more, surfaced as dashboards — free, and installable without building it yourself.
Custom objects and fields to "identify issues" (A) is a build with no measurement attached. Exporting and checking outside Salesforce (D) is a one-off audit that tells the sales managers nothing next month.

https://appexchange.salesforce.com/appxListingDetail?listingId=a0N300000016cshEAA
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) is streaming IoT data from connected devices to a cloud database. Every 24 hours. 100,000 records are generated. NTO employees will need to see these records within Salesforce and generate weekly reports on it. Developers may also need to write programmatic logic to aggregate the records and incorporate them into workflows. Which data pattern will allow a data architect to satisfy these requirements, while also keeping limits in mind?
optionA: Bidirectional integration
optionB: Unidirectional integration
optionC: Virtualization
optionD: Persistence
explanation:
Persistence is the answer: store the IoT records in Salesforce objects (D). The third requirement forces it — developers need to aggregate the records in Apex and feed them into workflows, and external objects do not support Apex triggers and have a narrow automation surface, so virtualized data cannot carry that logic. Weekly reporting on persisted records is straightforward once they are objects.
That is an exception to Salesforce's default advice, which runs the other way: "Unless the data absolutely needs to reside in Salesforce, consider data virtualization with Salesforce Connect instead", because "More data in your organization ultimately leads to larger data volumes, which can adversely affect performance and add technical debt." Virtualization (C) would satisfy the reporting requirement on its own; it is the programmatic aggregation and workflow participation that rule it out here.
Bidirectional and unidirectional (A, B) describe which way data flows, not whether it is stored — they answer a different question than the one asked. At 100,000 records a day, load the persisted records with the Bulk API to keep API consumption in hand.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/decision-guides/data-integration
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_external_objects_considerations.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is concerned that data is being corrupted daily either through negligence or maliciousness. They want to implement a backup strategy to help recover any corrupted data or data mistakenly changed or even deleted. What should the data architect consider when designing a field-level audit and recovery plan?
optionA: Reduce data storage by purging old data.
optionB: Implement an AppExchange package.
optionC: Review projected data storage needs.
optionD: Schedule a weekly export file.
explanation:
Field-level audit and recovery means keeping the old values, not just the current ones, and keeping them long enough to recover from something noticed weeks later. That is a storage question before it is a tooling one, so projecting the storage the retained history and backup copies will consume is the design consideration the plan turns on (C).
Purging old data (A) is the opposite of what a recovery plan needs. A weekly export (D) has a seven-day blast radius and no field-level granularity — it restores a record as it was last Saturday, not the one field somebody corrupted on Wednesday.
Be aware the item is loose. Option B, an AppExchange backup package, is how most orgs actually get granular field-level recovery, and it answers "what should the architect consider" nearly as directly as C does. C is keyed because it names a planning input rather than a product, but the two are not cleanly separated by the stem.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000383595&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.admin_exportdata.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Item defect: distractor B (an AppExchange backup package) is a reasonable answer to "what should the architect consider" for granular field-level recovery, and nothing in the stem separates a planning input from a tooling choice.

question: A national nonprofit organization is using Salesforce to recruit members. The recruitment process requires a member to be matched with a volunteer opportunity. Given the following: 1. A record is created in Project__c and used to track the project through completion. 2. The member may then start volunteering and is required to track their volunteer hours, which is stored in VTOTime__c object related to the project. 3. Ability to view or edit the VTOTime__c object needs to be the same as the Project__c record. 4. Managers must see total hours volunteered while viewing the Project__c record. Which data relationship should the data architect use to support this requirement when creating the custom VTOTime__c object?
optionA: Lookup Field on Project__c to VTOTime__c displaying a list of VTOTime__c in a related list.
optionB: Lookup field on VTOTime__c to Project__c with formula field on Project__c showing Sum of hours from VTOTime__c records.
optionC: Master-Detail Field on VTOTime__c to Project__c with roll-up summary field on Project__c showing sum of hours from VTOTime__c records.
optionD: Master-Detail field on Project__c to VTOTime__c showing a list of VTOTime__c Records in a related list.
explanation:
Two of the four requirements pick the relationship between them. Access parity — VTOTime__c must be viewable and editable exactly as its Project__c is — comes free with master-detail, because detail records "inherit the master's sharing and security settings". Total hours on the Project record needs a roll-up summary, and roll-up summary fields require a master-detail relationship. Both point at C.
The direction matters and options D and A get it backwards: the master-detail field lives on the detail object, so it belongs on VTOTime__c pointing at Project__c, not the reverse. And a formula field on Project__c (B) evaluates against its own record — it cannot sum values across child records, which is precisely the job roll-up summary exists for.

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Which two statements are accurate with respect to performance testing a Force.com application?
optionA: All Force.com applications must be performance tested in a sandbox as well as production.
optionB: A performance test plan must be created and submitted to Salesforce customer support.
optionC: Applications with highly customized code or large volumes should be performance tested.
optionD: Application performance benchmarked in a sandbox can also be expected in production.
explanation:
Salesforce requires approval before you load-test the platform, and the requirement is concrete: "Submit an LAP request for approval at least one week before the testing date", with a test plan document, dates, sandbox org id, business scenario and justification. "All tests must be pre-approved. Unapproved testing is subject to throttling or blocking." That settles B. And the applications worth putting through this are the ones whose behaviour is not already known — heavy custom code, or large data volumes (C).
Option A is not merely an overstatement; it describes something Salesforce forbids. "Because Salesforce is a multitenant platform, performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox for testing", and "scale tests are only permitted in sandboxes." Option D fails for the reason a full copy sandbox is specified in the first place: a sandbox with different data volumes is not a predictor of production.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2020/09/introduction-to-performance-testing

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation rejected option A with "not all apps must be tested in both environments", which leaves a learner believing production performance testing is sometimes required. Salesforce does not permit performance testing in production at all — it is sandbox-only, and every test needs prior approval.

question: Universal Containers would like to remove data silos and connect their legacy CRM together with their ERP and with Salesforce. Most of their sales team has already migrated to Salesforce for daily use, although a few users are still on the old CRM until some functionality they require is completed. Which two techniques should be used for smooth interoperability now and in the future.
optionA: Replicate ongoing changes in the legacy CRM to Salesforce to facilitate a smooth transition when the legacy CRM is eventually retired.
optionB: Specify the legacy CRM as the system of record during transition until it is removed from operation and fully replaced by Salesforce.
optionC: Work with stakeholders to establish a Master Data Management plan for the system of record for specific objects, records, and fields.
optionD: Do not connect Salesforce and the legacy CRM to each other during this transition period, but do allow both to interact with the ERP.
explanation:
Two systems are live and both can write, so the first thing to settle is who is right today: naming the legacy CRM the system of record for the transition period (B) removes the ambiguity while the remaining users are still on it. The second is who will be right tomorrow, per object and per field, as functionality moves across — that is what an MDM plan agreed with stakeholders gives you (C), and it is the part that survives the legacy system's retirement.
Replicating legacy changes into Salesforce (A) is a mechanism you might well implement, but it presumes the authority question is already answered. Refusing to connect the two CRMs (D) is a routing rule, not a governance decision, and it leaves the ERP mediating conflicts nobody has adjudicated.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the integration mechanisms rather than ranking these choices.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/decision-guides/data-integration
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Universal Containers (UC) is building a Service Cloud call center application and has a multi system support solution. UC would like or ensure that all systems have access to the same customer information. What solution should a data architect recommend?
optionA: Make Salesforce the system of record for all data.
optionB: Implement a master data management (MDM) strategy for customer data.
optionC: Load customer data in all systems.
optionD: Let each system be an owner of data it generates.
explanation:
"All systems have access to the same customer information" is a consistency requirement, and consistency needs an arbiter. An MDM strategy supplies one: a golden customer record with survivorship rules deciding which system's value wins for each attribute, which every system then reads (B).
Declaring Salesforce the system of record for everything (A) is a decision made before looking at which system is actually authoritative for which data. Loading the customer data into every system (C) creates the copies that drift. Letting each system own what it generates (D) is a reasonable-sounding rule that reproduces exactly the silos the stem is complaining about — the customer's address exists in three places and no rule says which one is current.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents integration mechanisms rather than naming MDM as the answer here.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://architect.salesforce.com/decision-guides/data-integration

question: NTO (Northern Trail Outlets) has a complex Salesforce org which has been developed over past 5 years. Internal users are complaining abt multiple data issues, including incomplete and duplicate data in the org. NTO has decided to engage a data architect to analyze and define data quality standards. Which 3 key factors should a data architect consider while defining data quality standards? Choose 3 answers:
optionA: Define data duplication standards and rules
optionB: Define key fields in staging database for data cleansing
optionC: Measure data timeliness and consistency
optionD: Finalize an extract transform load (ETL) tool for data migration
explanation:
Defining quality standards means naming the dimensions you will hold the data to and how each is measured. Duplication standards and matching rules (A) define what counts as the same record. Timeliness and consistency (C) cover how current a value must be and whether the same fact is recorded the same way everywhere. Completeness and accuracy (E) cover whether required information is present and correct — the two complaints the stem actually names.
Picking key fields in a staging database (B) and choosing an ETL tool (D) are migration decisions. They matter, but they belong to how data moves, not to what "good" means, and neither would appear in a standards document.
This is a definitional item drawn from general data-governance practice rather than a Salesforce rule.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm

question: (Variant) NTO has decided that it is going to build a channel sales portal with the following requirements: 1. External resellers are able to authenticate to the portal with a login. 2. Lead data, opportunity data and order data are available to authenticated users. 3. Authenticated users many need to run reports and dashboards. 4. There is no need for more than 10 custom objects or additional file storage. Which community cloud license type should a data architect recommend to meet the portal requirements?
optionA: Customer community.
optionB: Lightning external apps starter.
optionC: Customer community plus.
optionD: Partner community.
explanation:
Leads, opportunities, and orders are sales objects, and the Partner Community licence is the external licence that carries them along with reports and dashboards in the site (D). That combination is what a channel sales portal for resellers needs, and it is the line that separates this licence from the customer-facing ones.
Customer Community and Customer Community Plus (A, C) are built for service — cases, knowledge, orders — and do not extend to leads and opportunities. Lightning External Apps Starter (B) is sized for custom apps rather than CRM sales objects with reporting.
The stem's fourth requirement — no more than 10 custom objects and no extra file storage — is there to tell you the cheaper external licences are not being ruled out by object count, so the sales objects and reporting are what decide it.
Licensing is packaged commercially and changes often, so confirm the current Experience Cloud licence comparison before relying on this.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: DreamHouse Realty has an integration that creates records in a Salesforce Custom Object. The Custom Object has a field marked as required on the page layout. DreamHouse Realty has noticed that many of the records coming from the external system are missing data in this field. The Architect needs to ensure this field always contains data coming from the source system. Which two approaches should the Architect take? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Set up a Validation Rule to prevent blank values.
optionB: Create a Workflow to default a value into this field.
optionC: Mark the field required in setup at the field level.
optionD: Blame the customer's external system for bad data.
explanation:
Required on a page layout is a UI rule. It applies to the users looking at that layout and to nothing else, so an integration writing through the API sails past it — which is exactly what is happening here.
Both keyed options work at a level the API cannot bypass. Marking the field required at the field level makes it universally required, and a universally required field "must have a value whenever a record is saved within Salesforce, the Lightning Platform API, Connect Offline, Salesforce for Outlook, the Self-Service portal, or automated processes" (C). A validation rule rejecting blank values (A) runs on every save path too, and gives a message naming the problem.
Defaulting a value when the field is blank (B) makes the records look complete while losing the fact that the source system sent nothing — the opposite of ensuring the data comes from the source. Option D is not an approach.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_universally_required_field_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
